Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder

vaginismus · exclude a body cause, then treatIs it pelvic floor tightening with fear of pain, or a cause the examination finds?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Penetration difficulty, pain, fear of pain or a tightening pelvic floor about 6 months distress GPPPD (genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder), the term that took in vaginismus
  • Inspect the vulva cotton swab map one-finger pelvic floor check test any discharge no body cause first
  • Pelvic floor physical therapy psychotherapy such as CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) psychoeducation, combined, not stepped
What it is

One or more of: penetration difficulty, pain, fear of pain, pelvic floor tightening on the attempt

About 6 months clinically significant distress no better explanation

Driver

Symptoms typically from levator ani (pelvic floor) dysfunction involuntary contraction when a finger is inserted Naming noteBecause symptoms typically come from levator ani dysfunction, the term levator ani syndrome is increasingly used in place of vaginismus.

Triggers

History of abuse non-modifiable anxiety disorders, relationship conflict, cultural taboos; not present in every patient

Can also follow a vulvar infection such as candidiasis, a gynecologic problem such as endometriosis, or pregnancy

Chain

Pelvic floor muscle spasm genito-pelvic pain difficulty with penetration

Examination typically normal apart from a tight pelvic floor

Insights

Normal tissue a pelvic floor that contracts on one finger GPPPD when about 6 months with distress; an active finding treat that cause first

Anxiety only about penetration not GAD (generalized anxiety disorder); pain without preoccupation not somatic symptom disorder

Criteria and course, part by partdetail behind the chain
Criterion APersistent or recurrent trouble with one or more of four: penetration during intercourse; marked vulvovaginal or pelvic pain with intercourse or attempts; marked fear or anxiety about that pain before, during or after penetration; marked tensing of the pelvic floor on the attempt
DurationAbout 6 months or longer in the listing used here; Merck Manual gives the DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision) version as at least 6 months
ExclusionsNot better explained by a nonsexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress such as partner violence, or other major stressors; not due to a substance, a medication or another medical condition
Risk factorsAbuse, anxiety disorders, relationship conflict, cultural taboos; some patients have none
SecondaryAfter a vulvar infection such as candidiasis, a gynecologic problem such as endometriosis, or pregnancy
2Urgent risks
SafetyPartner violence: ask about it directly, in private

If abuse is disclosed or suspected, choose a check of her immediate risk and a safety plan made with her.

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
VulvodyniaVulvar pain or burning3 months or more; vulvar burning or stinging, not vaginal; no identifiable cause; the swab maps it Guideline detailNBME calls vulvodynia vulvar, not vaginal, pain not typically provoked by penetration; the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) also lists provoked, insertional forms, so the page separates them by where the problem sits: vulvar skin mapped by the swab versus a contracting pelvic floor.
Vaginal candidiasisRecent antibiotics, diabetes, immunosuppressionRed, swollen vulva and vagina; thick white discharge; organisms on microscopy
Worry about a range of topics6 months or more of excessive, hard-to-control worry plus 3 more symptoms; anxiety not limited to penetration
Preoccupied with symptoms; repeated visitsMore than 6 months; disproportionate thoughts, anxiety or time and energy on symptoms that distress or disrupt daily life, beyond attempted penetration
Posttraumatic stress disorderTrauma, then intrusive memories or nightmares; may avoid reminders1 month or more of symptoms; intrusions and avoidance tied to the trauma, not only to penetration
Female sexual interest/arousal disorderLittle interest or arousal; no pain6 months; at least 3 of 6 symptoms; distress
Genitourinary syndrome of menopausePostmenopausal burning and drynessMay show pale, dry tissue (may look normal in early menopause)
Lichen sclerosusBurning, dryness, itchingVisible skin changes; biopsy if needed
EndometriosisDeep pain; painful periods commonCul-de-sac nodularity on rectovaginal examination
Low mood, lost interest2 weeks, five symptoms; low mood or anhedonia beyond sex
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Normal vulva; pelvic floor contracts on one fingerGPPPDPelvic floor physical therapy with CBT
Swab reproduces vulvar burning; normal skin, no yeastVulvodyniaGentle vulvar care, physical therapy
Began after a treated yeast infection; microscopy clearStill GPPPD: active infection excludedTreat the GPPPD, not the yeast
Discharge, burning or odorVaginitis such as candidiasispH testing and microscopy
Deep pain with painful periodsEndometriosis, not an entry problemRectovaginal examination
Postmenopausal; pale, dry tissueGenitourinary syndrome of menopauseLubricants or moisturizers first; low-dose vaginal estrogen for moderate to severe symptoms (most effective)

Pause point. The bait: vulvodynia because both hurt at the entrance, or generalized anxiety disorder because she is anxious. Vulvodynia is vulvar pain the swab maps and does not explain a pelvic floor that clamps against penetration; anxiety confined to penetration is not generalized anxiety.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder Symptoms – one or more of penetration difficulty, marked pain with attempts, marked fear of that pain, or marked pelvic floor tightening on the attempt · Duration – about 6 months or longer Guideline detailCriteria as listed by the University of British Columbia Sexual Health Research group; Merck Manual Professional gives the DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision) version as at least 6 months with significant distress. · Distress – clinically significant · Exclusions – no nonsexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress such as partner violence, or major stressor explains it better; no substance, medication or medical cause
7Treatment
1

Primarycombined, not stepped

Pelvic floor physical therapy

Teaches pelvic muscle relaxation, sometimes with biofeedback; considered an effective intervention.

2

Primaryalongside

Psychotherapy such as CBT; sex therapy

Aims at fear and anxiety about pain; CBT is strongly recommended.

3

Primaryalongside

Psychoeducation

A primary part of treatment.

4

Addtight pelvic muscles

Sequential vaginal dilators

Self-dilation devices; part of multidisciplinary care. Guideline detailMultidisciplinary care can also include relationship and sexual counseling, lubricants and onabotulinumtoxinA injection.

5

Adjunctpain with sex, any time

Topical lidocaine before sex

For a short time only.

Treatment by diagnosis
DiagnosisChooseNot
GPPPDPelvic floor physical therapy with CBTAntifungal when microscopy is clear
Genitourinary syndrome of menopauseLubricants or moisturizers first, often enough for mild symptoms; low-dose vaginal estrogen, the most effective, for moderate to severeStopping at lubricants when symptoms stay moderate to severe
Lichen sclerosusUsually topical steroids
VulvodyniaGentle vulvar care, physical therapyVestibulectomy first: only after nonsurgical options fail, pain localized to the vestibule
EndometriosisOptions such as nonopioid analgesics, combined oral contraceptives or progestogens; laparoscopic excision
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
On topical lidocaineKeep it short term
Postmenopausal; symptoms stay moderate to severe on lubricantsLow-dose vaginal estrogen
Vulvodynia; nonsurgical options tried and failed; pain localized to the vestibuleVestibulectomy may be effective
Practice
  1. 26-year-old woman, 8 months of pain at the vaginal opening with every attempt at intercourse fear before each attempt; distressed Never had a pelvic examination T 36.8 °C · HR 78/min · anxious; asks to go slowly → Vulvar inspection, cotton swab testing and a single-digit examination → entry pain is examined first: inspection looks for a body cause, the swab maps vestibular pain and one finger finds a tight pelvic floor
  2. 27-year-old woman, 7 months unable to have intercourse began after a treated yeast infection dreads attempts; pelvic floor clamps down distressed; wants intercourse with her partner afebrile; vulva, vitals normal; no discharge or yeast · anxious · contracts on one-finger examination → Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder → fear and pelvic floor tightening for about 6 months with distress; it can follow a vulvar infection, and a clear microscopy excludes active infection
  3. 22-year-old woman, 1 year unable to have intercourse or insert a tampon fears the pain; muscles clamp down distressed; wants intercourse with her partner afebrile; vulva, vitals normal · swab test painless · microscopy normal · pelvic floor contracts on one finger · anxious → Pelvic floor physical therapy with cognitive behavioral therapy → genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder: treatment is multimodal, aimed at the pelvic floor and the fear
  4. 25-year-old woman, 9 months unable to tolerate intercourse or a speculum tenses and pulls away as the speculum nears T 37.0 °C · BP 114/72 mm Hg · vulva and vestibule normal · swab test painless · microscopy normal · anxious → Involuntary contraction of the pelvic floor muscles → symptoms typically result from levator ani dysfunction: it contracts on attempted penetration; the tissue itself is normal
  5. 38-year-old woman, 4 months of vulvar burning, most of the day with or without sex; intercourse, tampons possible vulva normal: no discharge, redness or skin change cotton swab reproduces the burning pelvic floor relaxed · no yeast · afebrile, menses normal; euthymic → Vulvodynia → vulvar burning most of the day, with or without sex, for at least 3 months with no identifiable cause (normal skin, no yeast); it is not a penetration problem, and 4 months is short of the roughly 6 months GPPPD needs
  6. 24-year-old woman, 4 days of vulvar itching and painful intercourse no pain with sex before this week finished amoxicillin for sinusitis 1 week ago vulva and vagina red, swollen · thick white discharge · T 37.0 °C · calm, euthymic → Vaginal candidiasis → redness, swelling and thick white discharge after antibiotics; microscopy of the discharge confirms, and 4 days is far short of the 6 months GPPPD needs
  7. 35-year-old woman, 8 months without interest in sex no sexual thoughts; never initiates; usually unreceptive little excitement during sex; distressed no pain or fear with penetration Sleeps well; enjoys work, hobbies afebrile, vitals normal · pelvic floor relaxed · euthymic, full affect → Female sexual interest/arousal disorder → at least 3 of the 6 interest and arousal symptoms for 6 months with distress; no pain, and no low mood or anhedonia beyond sex
  8. 58-year-old woman, last menstrual period 7 years ago 1 year of vaginal dryness and burning with intercourse lubricants help only briefly wants to stay sexually active vaginal tissue pale and dry · no discharge · pelvic floor relaxed, nontender · afebrile; euthymic → Low-dose vaginal estrogen → pale, dry postmenopausal tissue: vaginal estrogen is the most effective therapy for symptomatic women
How NBME framed it: question 1

23-year-old woman at a follow-up visit for an oral contraceptive refill sexually active with two male partners; pain has kept her from vaginal intercourse anxious ahead of sexual activity; feels her pelvic floor tighten and block penetration has also been unable to use tampons No history of sexual trauma vital signs normal · speculum hard to advance on pelvic examination

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Generalized anxiety disorder: she is anxious; but that needs 6 months or more of excessive worry about a range of topics with three more symptoms; hers is specific to penetration.
  • Somatic symptom disorder: the complaint is pain; but outside attempted penetration she shows no excessive preoccupation or repeated health-seeking.
  • Vaginal candidiasis: it is associated with vaginismus; but it typically shows vulvar and vaginal redness, swelling and thick white discharge, and the stem gives no antibiotics, diabetes or immunosuppression.
  • Vulvodynia: both hurt at the entrance; but NBME calls it vulvar, not vaginal, pain that is not typically provoked by penetration (the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists also describes provoked, insertional forms); it does not explain a pelvic floor that contracts to prevent penetration.

Down to two: vaginismus or vulvodynia. Vaginismus: pain, anxiety before sex and a pelvic floor that tightens to block penetration, with a speculum that is hard to advance. DSM-5 now calls it genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder; the stem gives no duration and uses the older term.

Transferable rule

When penetration hurts or fails, examine first: inspection looks for a body cause, microscopy tests any discharge, the swab maps vestibular pain and one finger checks the pelvic floor. Difficulty with one or more of penetration, pain, fear of pain or a pelvic floor that tightens, for about 6 months with distress and no body cause, is genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, treated with pelvic floor therapy and psychotherapy together.
